subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLE TRANSPORT ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today we are studying Bill C-19, an Act respecting motor vehicle transport by extra-provincial undertakings. Significantly enough, this Bill will replace the Motor Vehicle Transport Act of 1953-54. This statute, which relates to the interests of the trucking industry and inter-provincial bus companies, will be replaced by a series of new deregulation criteria which, I might point out, have to do only with the trucking industry. Still I hasten to add that it is too much anyway, for all people affected by this Bill do not want any part of this Conservative initiative.
Considering the uproar triggered by Bill C-18, we would have thought that the Government would have been farsighted enough to appreciate the fact that it had to be extremely careful and hesitant in its attempt to turn the Canadian transport system upside down. No, Sir, the message did not get through! Right on the heels of the mess it created with Bill C-18, here it goes again with Bill C-19 which is no better than the other one. Most regretfully and notwithstanding my deep admiration and esteem for the Parliamentary Secretary, I must say I cannot fathom whatever motive made the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) decide to miss this opportunity to introduce his own Bill. This utterly cavalier attitude on the part of the Minister of Transport is unacceptable. If he really has the interests of his Department at heart, if he feels that legislation before the House is important and deserves priority, he should be right here to defend his own Bills.
He made it a point to stay away from the House throughout the study of and debates on Bill C-18, and now he insults this institution by choosing not to be here to defend this second Bill introduced in the same week.
In my judgment, what needs to be said is that Bill C-19 is bound to have a strong impact on one of Canada's major industry. Indeed Figures for last year, 1986, show that this industry did about $8 billion worth of business and had over
50,000	people on its payrolls. Trucks carry about 40 per cent of all goods in Canada and about half of our exports to the United States.
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
So we are looking at one of the prime movers of the Canadian economy. Like the rest of us this industry had its ups and downs in the early 80s due to the recession, but it managed to pull through and continued to provide thousands of jobs throughout Canada for dedicated workers who have been able to earn quite a decent living thanks to the trucking industry. This is why, as we speak, operators, owners, interest groups and experts in the road transport industry have serious doubts about the changes the Conservative Government seeks to introduce by way of this Bill.
Together let us have a look at the propositions which, according to people who work in that sector, seriously threaten the very survival of hundreds of Canadian road transport companies, not just one or two. The Government is suggesting that we ought to drop the "public convenience and necessity" market criterion. This requirement, I may recall, has been in existence since 1954. It puts the burden of proof on the applicant, which means that if he is to have any chance at all of obtaining a licence, the applicant must prove that the service he intends to provide is absolutely necessary and that the general public will benefit. As a result, only truckers who provide a service for which there is a market can obtain a licence at the present time. The Government, allegedly for the sake of increasing competition, has decided to change all this and to substitute for this criterion the concept of "fit, willing and able". So what exactly does that mean? It means that from now on, the onus will be on existing licence holders to prove that adding a new carrier on a route where the service is already available will be a threat to the economic viability of that service. It will no longer be up to the party who wishes to provide a service to prove that what he is offering is essential. It will be up to the carriers already on the market and who want to prevent new carriers from entering the field to prove there are reasons why they should not do so. This kind of system makes no sense at all, since the parties who must prove that the other guy should not be licenced will be accused of being partial, and there is no way they can then submit evidence that will hold water and be objective, to keep the competitor from entering the market. The difference between the two systems is crystal-clear. Without a formal complaint, anyone who has a truck on four wheels and is willing, fit and able to operate the truck has a very good chance of obtaining a licence. It will be practically automatic. Anyone who wants to drive a truck will be able to get a licence.
I think we should consider the consequences of this kind of situation. The general effet on the Canadian market will be that more carriers will be competing, not for other markets but for the same market. If the purpose was to provide opportunities for expansion, one could consider it useful and appropriate to have more competition, but since it is the same market, the Canadian market, one wonders why the Canadian Government is taking this route. However, the additional competition from a few individuals who get a licence because they have a brand new truck will be negligible compared with the potential attraction of a more accessible Canadian market for the U.S. trucking industry giants who will compete with our domestic

February 5, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
trucking industry. We could expect foreign takeovers of Canadian surface carriers to increase rapidly over the next five years.
Look at what has happened in Canada in recent years. Since 1981, operating costs have increased 28 per cent, mainly owing to the taxes on gas and the shockingly exorbitant rates being charged for liability insurance. That is an area the Conservative Government has preferred to ignore. I think the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) should find out as soon as possible what is happening in this area, because liability insurance in this country has become a crushing burden, not only on the trucking industry but on a host of other sectors as well. Municipalities, companies and whole industries are being gouged by the insurance companies. This is a major problem, and although it is not within the purview of the Bill we are considering today, it is a very relevant issue for all these trucking companies.
Because of the increases the trucking industry must cope with and the fact that shipping rates have increased only 5 per cent, the net result or the profit margin, according to figures provided by the trucking industry, is down to 3 per cent. One of the lowest margins since the Second World War! US carriers, with a combined turnover far greater than that of the Canadian industry, could penetrate Canadian markets, lower their rates and absorb a few losses for one, two or three years, after which they could take over Canadian carriers who were unable to hold the distance. That is the danger of introducing this kind of access requirement when we are operating with this very low 3 per cent profit margin in Canada. Canadian carriers would not be able to lower their prices to compete with US truckers.
The Governement of Canada knows that. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and his predecessor, the present Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), were told as much by the Canadian trucking industry. Absolutely appalling though it may be, both the present Minister of Transport and his Conservative predecessor turned a deaf ear to these representations by the trucking industry.
We are talking about the danger that American companies might invade the Canadian market and impose cut-rate prices. Our main concern is that Combines Investigation Act provisions just cannot put a stop to that kind of competition. A few weeks ago the Conservative Government introduced a competition Bill which, admitedly, is a step in the right direction. But at the time the Official Opposition, the Liberal Party, stated that it was a practically toothless measure unlikely to go far enough to protect Canada's sound competitive market. Well, we now have the proof before us. The competition Bill introduced by the Conservatives a few weeks ago will do nothing to prevent American companies from imposing predatory rates. This is a basic question for us and, when this Bill gets to the parliamentary committee, my Liberal Party colleagues and I will move an amendment to Bill C-19 to make sure that it contains this kind of measure.
As it happens, this was part of the Canadian Trucking Association representations made as early as last December when it voiced its initial reaction to Bill C-19. Here is part of its important statement:
Competition Act provisions relating to predatory or discriminatory pricing have limited application to transportation. Bill C-19 is silent on the question of predation, meaning that the Canadian for-hire trucking industry is being thrust into a continental market-place increasingly dominated by a handful of billion dollar U.S. general freight carriers with absolutely no safeguards and certainly no assurances that those dominant continental truckers will provide a significant number of jobs in Canada while tapping key industrial markets.

Since July 1985 when the Government released its deregulation policy paper entitled Freedom to Move, four Canadian motor carriers have already been taken over by two major American firms: Akron's Roadway of Ohio has bought Arkena Express Lines of Toronto, and Overland's Yellow Freight of Kansas has bought three regional trucking firms of Windsor in Ontario.
So the process is already under way. It is quite possible, in fact not only quite possible but absolutely certain, according to people who know this sector, that the situation will grow worse and that Canada's trucking industry will be litterally swallowed by American interests.
I just cannot understand how this Conservative Government, stubbornly persevering in this course which is both absolutely pointless and detrimental to Canadian interests, can introduce such a Bill which surrenders outright to the Americans the whole Canadian trucking industry. The Conservative Government is prepared to sacrifice to American interests the jobs of some 50 000 Canadian workers, to pursue this pointless and certainly dangerous dream of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who had no idea of what he was getting into when he agreed to start discussing free trade with the President of the United States.
Concerning the strategy of major American corporations, Mr. Gerry Reimer, vice-president of Reimer Express Lines of Winnipeg said, and I quote:

American companies can come here and cut rates to smithereens for a year or two and all domestic truckers will be gone.

It is one of the senior officer of a Canadian company who said that, and he is not the only one. Mr. John Kennedy, president of Kingsway Transport of Rexdale in Ontario added, and I quote:

There is no question deregulation will have a devastating impact on the financial condition of the Canadian motor carrier industry. It will ultimately result in waves of mergers, buy-outs and bankruptcies.
February 5, 1987

These testimonies are not statements made by Members of the Opposition to embarrass the Government. They were made by people who operate daily in the Canadian trucking industry and who feel their industry being jeopardized by the incompetence and childishness of this Conservative Government. This situation is utterly unacceptable.
To emphasize the seriousness of possible foreign take-overs,
I urge the House to compare the difference between the turnovers of some American and Canadian firms. The biggest trucking firm in Canada, or rather Quebec is the Brazeau company with a turnover of $160 million in 1985. Kingsway Transport Limited, from Rexdale, Ontario, one of the biggest trucking firms in Canada, had a turnover of $250 million in 1985.1 repeat: The biggest in Quebec, $160 million; one of the biggest in Canada, $250 million. On the other hand, Roadway Express, the biggest trucking firm in the United States, had a turnover which exceeded $4 billion in 1985. It is easy to realize the enormous financial power which huge American corporations can exert. What is likely to happen in Canada is already happening in the United States, and this is a blind and stupid obstination on the part of the Conservative Government that we just cannot understand.
Deregulation in the United States has resulted in increased concentration and brought about, not increased competition, but reduced competition. Well, we suggest that the same thing will happen in Canada. We must stop this slavish and mindless aping of the Americans. What they did failed to benefit the American economy, so why should it benefit ours? There are some eloquent examples. Ever since the 1980 U.S. Motor Carrier Act came into effect, marking the start of deregulation of the trucking industry in the United States, the major companies have been expanding their operations.
In fact, the four giants, which are Roadway Express, Consolidated Freightway, Yellow Freight and United Parcel Services, have increased their share of the U.S. market by 24 per cent. This clearly shows that these companies can, and will, quickly increase their market share. If we open the gates wide as the Conservative Government, in its innocence, intends to do, these companies will come and increase their market share in Canada, gobble up Canadian companies and lay off hundreds if not thousands of Canadian workers who are earning a decent living in the trucking industry in Canada.
It is clear the federal Government is using this Bill to make it easier for these U.S. companies to operate on the Canadian market. When the Government says it wants to increase competition, I think there is a very real risk that most of this competition will not come from other Canadian companies, which would at least be some consolation, but from the U.S. giants, and that Canadian companies that are making a decent profit today will be face with the choice of closing down, laying off their workers or selling out to the Americans.
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
As the Executive Director of the Canadian Trucking Association, Mr. Ken McLaren, said so eloquently, and I quote:

Mr. Ken MacLaren said that this legislation, Bill C-19, the one that we are discussing today is like "letting Attila the Hun and Genghis Khan loose to feed on Canadian companies".

I see that the Minister is smiling at this comment, and I can understand him because this situation is one which amuses the Conservatives, but saddens tens, if not hundreds and thousands, of truckers who fear that, because of their irresponsible attitude, the Conservatives run the risk of giving away to the Americans a major Canadian industry. It is a well-known fact that the American companies are bigger and more monopolistic than ours. Indeed, we have to admit that the dynamic infrastructure which links the major American centres and the terminus network put up many years ago by the American companies make for a most effective system. Then, there is the fact that the Americans have a road network of no less than 860 highways linking various American metropolitan markets of over one million inhabitants. How many Canadian centres have a population of over one million? I repeat that there are 860 American cities with a population of about or over one million while we have only three in Canada. It is obvious that the American highway network gives the American companies an edge over the Canadian companies.
In addition, the increased difference between our two taxation systems since the major reform introduced in the United States in 1986 favours the American companies. As we know, American companies pay proportionately lower taxes because of the changes to the rules on vehicle depreciation in the United States. The America pay much lower taxes on gasoline and the American Governments intervene much less often in labour relations. Because of all these factors, it is clear that the American companies are much better off than Canadian companies in the trucking industry. We believe that, in all decency and to be fair to the trucking industry, the Conservative Government has no right to introduce this reform before the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has completed his tax reform and enabled the Canadian trucking industry to compete on an equal footing with American truckers. To proceed now with the deregulation of trucking in Canada when, for the second time, the Minister of Finance is drawing back from the promised tax reform because he does not have enough courage and conviction to go ahead with it is quite unthinkable. In my opinion, to do so would rob the Canadian truckers and that would be unconscionable.
I believe that one of the provinces which could lose a lot under this Bill is Manitoba. Eight of the 14 largest Canadian trucking companies with over 10,000 workers are located in that province. The industry representatives of that province are very concerned and the president of the Manitoba Trucking

February 5, 198
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
Association, Mr. Roily Painchaud, had this to say about the situation:
Manitoba stands to lose more than most provinces if reform of the trucking industry fails to safeguard domestic routes from competition by giant U.S. firms.

As we can see, the Government was given a warning but failed to take the message seriously, and that is regrettable.
I can see two Members from the Province of Manitoba-the Hon. Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Duguay) and his colleague from Winnipeg-behind the curtain of the Conservative lobby. I hope they will take part in this debate and protect the interests of their constituents and their province because Bill C-19 may indeed prove to be very damaging to the Manitoba economy.

Indeed, I am looking forward to seeing the Hon. Member intervene in this debate and talk sense with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie). This legislation will be murder for the trucking industry in Manitoba. I am looking forward to hearing some of those members of the Conservative Party from Manitoba who have the courage to speak out against this terrible legislation.

Not only do the consequences of deregulation undermine the motor carriers' ability to compete against the Americans, they also put them at a disadvantage with respect to the railway companies because of a provision contained in the other Bill which is part of this diabolical Conservative Government project aimed at revamping the trucking industry, and I am talking about Bill C-18 which will force truckers to play second fiddle to rail carriers. I want to refer to the provisions concerning confidential contracts. The confidential rates mentioned in Bill C-18 will enable CN and CP Rail to hold secret negotiations with the shipper with a view to setting the rates. As a result, the shipper who deals with both companies will be in a position to pay lower freight rates. But this will also force road transport companies to reduce their rates just to remain competitive with railway companies with respect to goods that can be shipped either way. Let us keep in mind that the current trucking industry profit margin is barely 3 per cent. How can any one expect fair competition under such circumstances? It stands to reason that this additional competition from the railways will so squeeze the trucking concerns that here again we can expect to see many of them throw in the towel and sell out to Canadian or foreign interests.
The situation is getting more involved as we look into the safety implications of deregulation. Even with all the indications obtained from the Government, even with all the indications stemming from the American experience since 1980, the Conservative Government has chosen to overlook
that aspect. This Tory Government is turning a blind eye and making pious statements that there is no safety problem. They say they will never compromise on safety. But here are the facts: Since the U.S. Motor Carrier Act of 1980 went into force, there has been an 18 percent rise in accidents involving trucks in the United States. And there is no reason to believe the same thing will not happen in Canada with deregulation.
The fierce competition that was experienced in the United States following deregulation brought rates down, and trucking companies were forced to cut their costs. Wages went down, drivers had to work long hours and companies started to skimp on vehicle maintenance work. The result was that seven trucks out of ten were being driven around in the United States with unsafe equipment. And out of those seven trucks, 80 per cent belonged to new entrants on the American market since 1980.
The experience clearly points to the fact that deregulation makes it easier for one-truck, one-driver companies to enter the market and very often skimp on safety in order to be in a better position to compete with larger companies. Furthermore, such competition forces established companies to compromise on safety by reducing maintenance schedules, lenghthening driver working hours and extending the life cycle of pieces of equipment.
I therefore submit that by implementing Bill C-19, the Government is betraying the call of Canadians for greater road safety in Canada. We can easily expect the American experience will repeat itself in Canada and our roads will become less safe because of the Tory Government's irresponsible action.
For quite some time provincial ministers and representatives of the Canadian trucking industry have been asking for the implementation of a national safety code. In addition, they have also asked that it be put in place before or at least upon the Bill coming into force. But we find that to date, the Government has totally ignored those requests from the provincial authorities. The national road safety code would ensure that the American experience would not be repeated in Canada, or at least with the same degree of seriousness as in the United States.
And why such a delay? Because, in fact, the Tory Government that boasted of entertaining good relations in the area of federal-provincial exchanges did nothing in that area. There was a conference where pious wishes were expressed, but there really has been no formal agreement between Ottawa and the provinces. Why such a delay? For those truckers, and for all motor vehicle passengers in Canada, that delay means additional serious risk. I submit that risk should not be taken. There should be no compromise on safety when human lives are at stake because of a desire to enact post-haste deregulation in Parliament. The fact remains that these road transport companies, American mostly, did not respect safety measures and I would be very surprised indeed if in a similar context, without any constraint, Canadian companies would do any better. Had this Government any common sense at all I
February 5, 1987

suggest it would reconsider its structure and its strategy. The fact that the Government is prepared to put an industry which employs 50,000 Canadians through this kind of ordeal, perhaps leading to its demise, proves that it governs in the interest of a very small minority. In one fell swoop it may very well undo the work of several generations of people who built in this country a road transport industry which, besides being strong, happens to be competitive and provides a considerable number of well-paid jobs. In conclusion, Madam Speaker, I will say that this Government is running the risk of undermining all these past efforts only to please the American Government which seeks yet another concession from the Conservative Government in the free trade negotiation process. I think this is quite unacceptable. I think it is absolutely shameful, and the Liberal Party will fight to the end to prevent the Conservatives from crawling once again before the Americans.

subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLE TRANSPORT ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie that Bill C-19, an Act respecting motor vehicle transport by extra-provincial undertakings, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLE TRANSPORT ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to be the lead-off speaker for the NDP on Bill C-19. However, I must say it is like a time warp for me. As a member of the Ontario Legislature some 11 years ago I was a member of a select committee charged with studying regulation or deregulation of trucking in Ontario. Having gone from that House to this House I now find myself
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
back where I started, debating once again the merits of regulating or deregulating the trucking industry, not just in Ontario this time but across Canada.
That time spent on the select committee gave me a very broad understanding of the industry in Ontario and its importance to the people of that province. We travelled around the province to many communities, in fact many more communities than the committee of this House did in its study of the White Paper Freedom to Move. You will remember that the Standing Committee on Transport went to three communities, Halifax, Winnipeg and Vancouver, and held hearings in Ottawa as well. While I do not remember the number of communities we went to in Ontario during the 1976 hearings, it was considerable. We went through a number of communities in northern Ontario to get a sense of what trucking meant to those towns and villages and the people who reside in them so that we could understand the economic impact of changes in the regulations. Quite frankly, it appears to me that nothing has changed. Trucking is vitally important to them. It is their mainstay and they need the protection of regulation because they will not get any protection through freeing up the industry.
What I would like to do today is give you and Members of this House, and those Canadians who happen to be watching, an idea of the state of the trucking industry in Canada. I will then go into some specific examples of the impact of deregulation in the U.S. on their carriers and workers and communities, as well as the impact in Canada, and my assessment of the over-all impact on Canadians of this particular Bill.
The Canadian trucking industry, for several reasons specific to its structure in Canada, will be particularly hard hit by deregulation. While the devastating impact that deregulation had on the American trucking industry, i.e., massive lay-offs, bankruptcies, increasing concentration, loss of service to the hinterland, and so on, will be repeated in Canada, there is a real likelihood that because of the particular character of the industry here the consequences will be even more severe.
There are three features of the Canadian trucking industry which must be borne in mind when assessing the likely impact of deregulation. First, market size and orientation. Unlike the American market with its demographic concentrations, the Canadian market has only three cities with a population over one million. While the U.S. has 1,722 city pairs with a one million plus population, Canada has only six, with a huge gap between Quebec-Ontario and the west. Without regulation of the trucking industry in a form similar to what we have now there will be little incentive to maintain an east-west transportation system, the historical basis of our economic system.
An individual who is knowledgeable about the trucking industry, in a speech on October 25, 1985, to the Chartered Institute of Transport in Ottawa, Mr. John F. Kennedy of the Kingsway group of companies, gave this impression of the industry in Canada. He said that by the late 1970s it became very evident that while the Canadian trucking industry was trying to follow the growth pattern of its U.S. counterpart,

February 5, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
absolutely no thought was ever given to the fact that the Canadian market-place was completely different from that in the U.S. The industry simply failed to recognize that the major distinguishing market characteristic between the two nations is that Canada derives its economic strength from its natural resource base, whereas the United States generates its economic activity predominantly through its manufacturing base. In other words, Canada is mostly a truckload country while the U.S. is largely less than truckload or LTL.
The Canadian trucking industry also demonstrated an overall lack of perception regarding other significant differences between the Canadian and U.S. market-place which resulted in a massive under-utilization of hundreds of LTL terminal facilities across Canada. To begin with, for-hire trucking in Canada is estimated to be a $6 billion industry consisting of thousands of individual carriers, whereas in the United States the 10 largest carriers alone control close to $7 billion in annual freight revenues. The United States has 42 cities with a population over one million which produces a matrix of 861 major inter-city traffic arteries, whereas in Canada we only have three cities with over one million in population and a linear grid of three major city traffic arteries.
LTL weight expressed as a percentage of total weight is in the 60 per cent to 80 per cent range for most general commodity carriers in the U.S., while in Canada it is rare to find a major carrier which handles in excess of 30 per cent LTL by weight.
A further analysis of class one and two common carriers reveals that 42 per cent of all the freight handled in the U.S. is LTL, whereas in Canada LTL freight represents only 14 per cent of the over-all tonnage handled. The reason for these significant statistics is obvious when one considers that 25 major manufacturing centres in the U.S. provide the hub for all the movement of freight and generally LTL movements move in all directions from these hubs. Canada, on the other hand, has basically two major manufacturing centres and both are situated in eastern Canada. This dictates that the majority of LTL freight moves in one direction, that being east to west, and proportionately speaking there is a much smaller volume of LTL freight moving in the opposite direction.
Given this tremendous imbalance of LTL freight moving between eastern and western Canada, Canadian motor carriers have to maintain a relatively high proportion of truckload freight on eastbound lanes to offset fixed costs, and should the volume of truckload traffic decrease significantly many carriers would have to shut down their operations.
Our present regulatory system, with its control of market entry, pricing and commodity and destination restrictions, has intentionally created a pattern of cross-subsidization of traffic through the encouragement of transportation generalists. To cite an example given by the Canadian Trucking Association, a long-haul trucking company will give up perhaps 10,000 pounds of capacity and $20,000 in costs per trailer to move
general freight, for example, manufactured goods, from Ontario to the East or West in order to obtain backhaul which includes significant movement of perishable products such as refrigerated beef or fish. This pattern of accepting less than truckload could only occur where the competition was managed and there was a predictable return on investment, for example, through regulation.
The reduction or elimination of this regulatory control in the industry would encourage the super efficient and the transport specialist to the point of driving the transport generalist out of the market. The generalist would no longer have the incentive to haul LTL. With the demise of cross-subsidization and the generalist goes the historic east-west pattern of transportation. The economic logic of efficiency and deregulation will mean the demise of service for the regions and the smaller communities of the market centre.
That is exactly what we heard in 1976 when we toured northern Ontario. The smaller communities which do not have the volume coming in, let alone going out in terms of manufactured goods, are concerned that through deregulation they will be at the mercy of whichever carrier survives in a cutthroat market. To them deregulation means increased costs and reduced service.
When the United States introduced deregulation in the trucking industry in 1980 it did not have a much larger neighbour nearby with the geographic and economic capacity to enter and predominate in the transport industry, among other things. With all of the upheaval caused by deregulation the U.S. trucking industry did not face the additional distraction of competition from an economically stronger and better prepared international competitor. Canada clearly does.
With the erosion of our east-west trading and transportation systems through the economic logic of deregulation will come the flip side of the coin. The Canadian trucking industry will be beaten in the international competition for the north-south trade. The economic stakes are high. Presently half the value of Canadian-American trade travels by truck. That is one-half the value. This generates $1 billion in carrier revenue of which Canadian carriers reserve half. Loss in jobs, equipment purchase, foreign exchange earnings, and tax revenue and the potential loss for Canada is readily apparent.
In a study the Canadian Trucking Association notes that the impending danger from American competition comes not from Canadian inefficiency but from the inherent advantages enjoyed by the U.S. These advantages include the short haul extension which the Canadian market represents for American truckers. With the purchase or creation of several terminals in Canada the U.S. trucking company has access to the Canadian import and export trade. The reverse is not true.
State deregulation has not occurred to the same degree that is proposed in the Canadian provinces. Combined with the demographic differences, the U.S. trucker will have a much greater ease of entry than a Canadian carrier into the U.S.
February 5, 1987

The penetration of the Canadian market for the U.S. trucker will invariably mean a turn-around operation close to the border where backhauls are less important. For the Canadian trucker, on the other hand, the long haul means a trip deeper into the U.S. industrial heartland with a greater difficulty of obtaining backhauls to Canada.
U.S. truckers will have a greater ability to grant discounts and contract rates based on volume because more of this international traffic will be included with their domestic traffic. The high degree of American manufacturing and industrial subsidiaries in Canada, whose exports account for 50 per cent of all Canadian exports, will likely favour a single line service to the U.S. American trucking companies will have a distinct advantage in obtaining this trade, in part because of the discounts offered by U.S. truckers to the American parent company as part of an over-all agreement for the continental business of the parent.
In November of 1985 The Globe and Mail reported that U.S. trucking companies are expecting that Canadian trucking deregulation will mean a continental bonanza by giving them unrestricted access to the Canadian market, thus allowing them to offer non-stop Los Angeles to Vancouver or Miami to Toronto service. The Globe and Mail went on to note:
One area where the U.S. carriers are expected to make inroads is in the business currently going to private carriers. Last year, (1984) Canadian companies did about $5 billion worth of business in their private fleets, but with rates falling, they would be encouraged to shift to for-hire carriers.
U.S. carriers also expect to take business away from Canadians by signing deals with U.S. parent companies to transport the goods of the parent and its Canadian subsidiaries.
"That would settle the fate of a lot of things in Canada without Canadian companies getting a kick at the cat", Mr. Cope, (Executive Vice-President of the Ontario Trucking Association) said.
There is clearly the question of the vulnerability of the trucking industry in Canada. Given the likely demise of our historic east-west economic and transport system, weak as it is, and the impending domination of the north-south trade by the American trucking industry, there is a real concern that deregulation will quickly undermine an efficient but fragile domestic industry.
While reliable figures about the structure of the trucking industry and its financial position are not easy to come by, what figures are available portray an industry marked by many small firms and a few very large firms, all operating with a slender profit margin. The majority of the approximately
10,000	trucking carriers in Canada are small one to three truck operations with a small profit margin and an inability to weather a sustained reversal in business fortunes. Even among the very large trucking firms there historically has not been a pattern of large profits. An industry spokesman recently remarked that even in the best of times industry-wide profit levels are only around 3 per cent. In 1984, 22 per cent of companies reporting to the Ontario Trucking Association were still suffering losses.
Although the limited data available on the structure of the industry has not indicated an undue amount of market
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
concentration up until now, the first show of deregulation is already here. In 1985 specifically there were at least four major takeovers and mergers which were triggered in large part by the spectre of deregulation. Reimer Express Enterprises bought Inter-City Truck Lines in April to create one of the largest trucking companies in Canada. In August of that year Dominion Consolidated Truck Lines and Overland Express merged to create the largest trucking company in Ontario. The same month CP Express, Canada's largest road carrier, bought Pickard Moving and Storage. As well, Direct Transportation System was sold to Canadian Motorways, creating what The Globe and Mail described as the biggest shake-up in the industry so far.
The Globe and Mail quoted one industry spokesman as saying that the result of these developments is a concentration of the market in the hands of a few carriers which is inevitable under deregulation. He said that "Eventually, the Canadian market is going to be dominated by five or six big companies, and they are going to fight it out". Another industrial spokesman quoted by the same paper said that his company's decision to merge was influenced by the pending deregulation. He said that "In the United States and Australia large well-financed trucking companies have been the clear winners under a new regulatory environment. We are convinced this pattern will hold true in Canada".
The myth accompanying deregulation is that with the elimination of government's visible hand competition will reign free, the economy will revive, the consumer will again be sovereign, and there will be so many winners that those few losers who fell by the wayside by the process of natural economic selection will be grateful for the chance to be martyrs for efficiency. Indeed, the centrepiece of the statement by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) when he released his Freedom to Move paper was his declaration that the object of deregulation was to promote "flexibility, innovation and competitiveness".
Even if the impact of deregulation in Canada is no worse than what has happened since 1980 in the United States, the trucking industry as we know it will likely be left competitive and more concentrated than before. An American trade journal, Fleet Owner, noted:
The handful of nationwide LTL carriers is consolidating its hold on the market, as predicted prior to 1980 by deregulation opponents. While some 350, mostly LTL carriers have gone out of business or severely curtailed operations since mid-1960, the industry's 10 largest companies have substantially increased their market share. Last year (1983) those 10 companies controlled more than half of the industry's total profits.
Carrier overcapacity in the United States has become a crippling problem. The executive director of the Independent Truck Owner Operators Association, a strong proponent of deregulation prior to 1980, testified before congressional oversight hearings in 1983. He said, "The effects of the Motor Carrier Act of 1980 on the trucking industry and labour have been disastrous". Both the truck load and the LTL sectors were ravaged by deregulation with "the medium-sized carriers forced out of business through the destructive practices

February 5, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
engaged in by large carriers through the use of discounting tactics". He cited academic studies which predicted that after the initial shake-up of the industry has been completed there will be four or five giant nationwide LTL carriers, approximately 20 medium-sized regional LTL carriers and little else.
Let me point out a disturbing aspect of the process we have gone through. The Transport Committee had before it the White Paper Freedom to Move. We were allowed to travel to three Canadian cities to talk to Canadians about what they believe might be the effect of deregulation in their various sectors. However, we were not allowed to go to the United States to talk to truckers, airline officials and government officials to discover from them, first-hand, what the impact of deregulation has been on their industries.
Quite clearly, if we are to copy the rules of the game from the United States, we should at the very least have the opportunity to meet with them and find out how those rules have worked, if they have worked at all.
Let me refer again to Mr. Kennedy's speech regarding the U.S. situation. He said that if there is one particular thing that U.S. truck deregulation has taught us, it is that nothing can be cross-subsidized in the trucking business. There has been a tremendous increase in the number of truckload carriers on the one hand and a heavy concentration of large LTL carriers on the other. The losers are the regional and inter-regional carriers who have mixed truckload and LTL operations.
But at the same time the trucking industry is not the only business sector to feel the consequences of deregulation. The small and medium-sized manufacturing companies that do not have access to the LTL volumes required to take advantage of carrier discounts are left with the burden of having to pay higher freight charges in order to offset the lower rates being charged to ship the larger volume shippers.
He went on to say that the principle of "the larger shipper pays less and the smaller shipper pays more" has some serious implications for all Canadian businesses, not just for Canadian-based trucking companies. I suggest that this applies as much to the smaller communities between major cities as it does to the smaller business operations.
The irony of deregulation is that by opening the doors to unregulated competition, it promotes concentration. In the period following the passage of the Motor Carrier Act in 1980 in the United States, virtually anyone applying for an entry trucking permit received one, I presume as long as they were fit, willing and able. By 1983 there were some 11,000 new carriers competing, setting off rate wars that chopped truckers income by as much as 30 per cent. Thousands of independent truckers, some of whom had enjoyed a stable and prosperous livelihood prior to deregulation, and others who had invested their life savings to grab a share of free enterprise when they thought they heard opportunity knock in 1980, went out of business.
In 1983 The Wall Street Journal estimated that the numbers dwindled from nearly 300,000 to just 100,000 since the late 1970s. Commenting on the fatal price squeeze faced by the small independent truckers, a spokesman for the American Trucking Association said, "A lot of these guys are living off their depreciation. They are in a going-out-ofbusiness sale and they don't even know it".
Accompanying that increasing concentration of the American trucking industry were significant decreases in rates charged and industry profits brought on by deregulation. In 1983, profit levels were less than 3 per cent industry-wide and falling. Despite the ongoing economic recovery, 29 per cent of trucking companies lost money and an industry association estimated in late 1984 that as much as one carrier in five was a potential bankruptcy candidate. I wonder how many are still around.
Aside from bankruptcies, growing concentration, and industrial profit decline, trucking deregulation in the United States meant a sudden increase in truck terminal closings. In the spring of 1980 Philadelphia had 97 truck terminals in operation. By December, 1983, not even three years later, only 68 terminals remained open. In the same period, Boston, Kansas City, Pittsburgh and Cleveland also suffered a doubledigit net percentage decline. In Ohio, every major city except Columbus showed a net decline in terminal closings. With these closings came an accompanying loss of terminal-oriented jobs and a reduction of choice of shippers and fee scales. Of course, this means fewer competitors.
The threat posed by deregulation to the Canadian trucking industry will have several dire consequences for Canadian workers in the industry. Clearly, they will be among the most prominent of losers should this Bill be passed. They would face a career spectre of massive lay-offs, a decline of wages and benefits for those who remain, and a deterioration in their safety and working conditions.
There are an estimated 100,000 people working in the for-hire trucking sector, with approximately 80,000 of those classified as employees, that is, workers belonging to, or eligible to belong to unions. Another 285,000 Canadians work in the private trucking sector, driving or assisting in the driving of goods from companies who own the goods such as Stein-burgs or Carling O'Keefe. There are no accurate figures on the degree of unionization among the for-hire trucking sector, but it is estimated to be 60 per cent with the Teamsters, CBRT and GW, and BRAC as the predominant unions.
In the United States, deregulation has created a chaotic industrial relations environment, marked most prominently by the disappearance of hundreds of thousands of good paying jobs. It is estimated that over-all in the industry, between
250,000	and 300,000 union members have lost employment in recent years. Thousands more saw a generation of wage increases and working benefits rolled back as the trucking unions, principally the Teamsters, gave concession after concession back to the companies. The initial cause of this supply side industrial relations was the emergence of a large
February 5, 1987

number of non-union carriers freed of the restrictions of market entry and licence limitations. Since the trucking industry is labour intensive, this influx of lower cost carriers knocked the bottom out of the industry's wage structure and employment figures and the industry has been spiralling ever since.
There may be those in this country who believe that a reduction in wages will mean less cost to move goods. They forget, however, that it is those same unionized, decently paid employees who shop in their stores and buy those consumer goods. If they have less wages they will buy less and ultimately the store owner and operators will lose because of that reduction in earning ability. We should keep this in mind rather than assume that lower wages will mean a better situation nationally.
As a consequence, the ability of the trucking unions to ensure adequate working and living conditions for their members has been drastically sliced in the last five years. Wage reductions, wage freezes for extended periods, and deferral of negotiated payments until future dates are now the order of the day. Because of the wage sensitivity of the deregulated industry, a whipsaw effect has emerged; a wage concession in one company brings another, often deeper demand from another, until the cycle comes back to the initiating company that now demands a new wage concession "to remain competitive".
Other ominous emerging trends in the industry bargaining are reduction in holiday and vacation time, health and welfare and pension concessions, erosion of work jurisdiction rules, the double-breasting of unionized and non-unionized subsidiaries, two-tier wage structures, immensely decreased bargaining strength and vigorous efforts by non-union employees to keep unions out. Industry spokesmen in the U.S. have stated that while a smaller, cheaper and tamer workforce was not the primary reason for their support of deregulation, they now recognize it as its greatest blessing.
Meanwhile, thousands of former trucking employees remain on the outside staring in. Despite the proliferation of small, non-union trucking firms, there are not nearly enough jobs to make a serious dent in the unemployed truckers' ranks, even if most of the unemployed would be willing to take trucking jobs that would pay, in many cases, half their former wages and benefits. The U.S. economy has lost productive workers whose consumption needs and wants are a necessary pre-condition for an economic recovery. We certainly do not want that to happen in Canada.
One feared industrial relations consequence of trucking deregulation will be the forced conversion of company drivers into independent owner-operators. Instead of working under a collective agreement with a set wage, set benefits and an agreed upon work schedule, the driver would have to become a "tiny capitalist", with his own overhead, uncontrolled hours, and unstable income and benefit earnings. Not only does the company lessen its wage and compensation costs, but it also
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
destroys the bargaining strength of the unions by making the driver an employee, but by another name.
Aside from massive employment dislocation, trucking deregulation threatens safety on our highways. As in other industries, the regulation of trucking was designed to ensure that the nation receives safe, adequate and continuous service to all at reasonable rates. The issue of safety is tied to the issues of entry ease, level of competition, adequate wage and benefit levels and rate of return.
It is obvious that with the floodgates of comptetion being opened, the scramble for freightloads will force down the already narrow cost margin. Safety in trucking and elsewhere has historically been one of the most expendable items when profits and productivity are threatened. The erosion of trucking safety is a matter which will be very difficult to police in the absence of a regulated and financially stable industry.
Regardless of safety provisions, deregulation brings hazardous road conditions. Carriers who operate on a shoestring can hardly attend to matters of new tires or brake overhaul when they live, as a vast majority of them will, from shipment to shipment. Trucking companies will stay on the road longer as companies are forced to cut expenses to the bone. The quality of repair work and upgraded equipment will deteriorate in all but the most profitable of companies. Truckers, particularly small owner operators, will drive longer stretches and carry more overweight cargo as freight rate cutting forces them to accept any available assignment, thus increasing the danger to themselves and those with whom they share the highway.
In northwestern Ontario we have a lot of trucks on the road. They are there for a few reasons. From this side of Kenora, the eastern side of Kenora, through to Shabaqua Corners, which is just west of Thunder Bay, there are alternate routes. We have Highway 11 or Highway 17. From Shabaqua Corners to Systonens Corners, there is a single two-lane highway. From Thunder Bay to Nipigon there is a single two-lane highway. They are funnels, if you like, Madam Speaker, where all of the east-west highway trucking must take place. In addition, on all of those highways running through the north-west we have a very large concentration of pulpwood trucks, large trailer trucks hauling the harvest of our forests to the mills which are becoming located farther and farther away.
Over the last couple of years in northwestern Ontario we have had a number of very serious accidents involving pulp transport trucks. A number of lives of innocent people have been lost.
With deregulation there will be many more trucks on the road. There will be greater movement of goods from east to west by road rather than by rail. There is even talk of bringing grain from Manitoba and Saskatchewan to Thunder Bay by truck. As more of these operators, who have a dream and who are supposedly fit, willing and able, whatever that means, go

February 5, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
from load to load or contract to contract, they will be cutting corners.
What price will we have to pay on those northern highways for this increased traffic? What will be the pressures on the provincial Government to add to the road capacity and construct four-lane highways across northern Ontario? There will, of course, be pressure on the federal Government from the provinces to do the same thing. The federal Government is already contributing $50 million to upgrade the Yellowhead route in western Canada. There is no reason they would not be expected to pay to upgrade the Trans-Canada Highway through northern Ontario to standards equivalent to that of the prairies and southern Ontario.
I would like to give an example of the difference between regulating safety and the economics of the trade. New pulp truck trailers come with brakes on every set of wheels. There is one axle which is used only at a time when the truck has a load. I have learned through a constituent that the tendency is that when the brakes on that extra axle wear out they are not replaced. It is not required by regulation but is something the manufacturer adds. The operator uses them as long as they work but once they wear out the company cuts the brake cables and does not replace them. That is not against the law. However, it eliminates the truck's extra stopping power. That is the kind of thing which will happen as the trucking companies get squeezed and squeezed because of what will probably be cutthroat competition. They will check the manual and find that they must replace the brakes every 5,000 miles. You can be assured, Madam Speaker, they will not replace them at
4,000	miles even if they are showing some wear because the rules say "5,000 miles". In fact, I would not be surprised if they would wait for 5,020 miles or 5,100 miles before replacing them. They will squeeze those extra miles out. That is what we are concerned about.
We do not doubt that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) believes that safety is the number one criteria, but we must look at the economic factors. First, in this case it is the provincial inspection staff who will be examining the trucks. Certainly, in northwestern Ontario we do not see them often enough. They are not always out there. There are very few of them. What about the truckers who are taking the gamble? They have the bailiff almost knocking on the door and the bank calling every day. They have Esso or Gulf demanding payment of that $4,000 fuel bill. How far are they going to stretch it? What chances are they going to take in order to stay alive in the trucking business? That is what we are afraid of.
We are not against a redefinition of the rules of the road. We recognize that this is 1987 and we have to re-examine all of the rules under which we operate, all the regulations and all the laws. Laws which were written in 1950 do not necessarily apply to the technology of today. We are not against examination of regulation or against bringing them up to the 21st century.

As has been pointed out by several speakers, including our own critic on the matter, there are some very serious flaws in this Bill which were created because the Government cut off hearings and would not listen to many people in our country who have knowledge of the transportation industry. The Government insisted on pushing this Bill into Parliament over the objections and unheard arguments of people who are responsible for many sectors of the transportation industry in Canada, particularly the trucking industry.
If this legislation is enacted, it will dismantle a great deal of the legislation that has been built up through generations of often bitter experience. This Bill needs substantial reconsideration through consultation with those who work in the industry, such as the Canadian Truckers Association. The first aspect is the rather simplistic, even foolish, emphasis on changing immediately from the concept of public usefulness in a crowded jurisdiction to the principle of reverse onus, that is, that you must prove it is not needed, or anyone who can get in. Eventually, if you have a truck and a licence you will be in business.
Roads are provided at public expense and there is a limit to what can be done on them. In Toronto, roads are being continually repaired and sometimes widened to accommodate the growing traffic. If the traffic is allowed to grow without constraint, governments will not be able to keep up with the repair and maintenance of the roads.
The test of public utility has already failed. About 10 years ago the then Conservative Government of Ontario donated to Greyhound Bus some of the gravy runs which had been built up by a publicly owned corporation, Grey Coach, a subsidiary of the Toronto Transit Corporation. Without having done any of the spadework, Greyhound was allowed to take the runs between Windsor, Toronto, Buffalo and Sudbury. It does not have to serve the towns in between. It cut into the best revenues of Grey Coach, which built those runs through public employment and the fares and taxes of the public over several decades. Grey Coach is still obliged to serve the small towns, at a loss if necessary. Greyhound receives the benefit and Grey Coach pays the cost. Canadian workers, farepayers and
February 5, 1987

taxpayers are subsidizing an American corporation due to the generosity of former Premier William Davis to Greyhound Buslines.
We do not want such foolishness to become widespread, as it would through the passage of this legislation. U.S. truckers would have much greater use of Canadian roads than they now have. U.S. trucks would be able to take goods from Toronto through the United States, re-entering at Halifax, Winnipeg, or Vancouver. They would be able to use roads which cost less to build and maintain because of more favourable weather. They would be able to use fuels which are priced lower than the Government prices fuel in Canada. The taxes which they would have to pay would, in many cases, be lower than the taxes charged by provincial Governments in Canada for the maintenance of roads.
In other words, they can travel more cheaply east and west between Toronto and Winnipeg by using American roads. Canadian truckers are not allowed to do that. This Bill gives American truckers freedom to haul Canadian goods over American roads. Canadian truckers, however, have no corresponding right to use American roads and will be at a disadvantage.
As has been pointed out by those concerned with the industry, domestic and cross-border trucking should be dealt with separately rather than with one quick breath, as is attempted here. We should also study what is happening in the United States before we leap into their pattern. Some of the states are having second thoughts about the wonderful dream of deregulation. Their experience has been a sharply rising accident rate since regulations have been weakened. Several states are considering the reintroduction of regulation to a much greater extent than they thought they would need a few years ago. Before plunging into this, we should study what the Americans are doing. We should invite them to come and tell us what they are doing.
My Party wanted to bring experts from the United States, not to tell us what to do, but to tell us what their experience is. The Government, in a curious burst of anti-Americanism, refused to allow an American transportation expert to come to Canada to tell us what is happening in the United States. This anti-Americanism is very curious from the Government of a Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who professes to be such a close friend of the American President. Many people are wondering what uncomfortable truths would have been presented to the committee if American representatives had been allowed to speak. What fear of the truth caused the Government to shut them out? I believe we must look into that.
There are other matters we should consider before allowing such an open door to American trucks to operate in Canada. There must be some system of monitoring the arrangement, yet nothing adequate is provided for monitoring differences or disputes. Nothing is provided for arbitrating disputes. There is no effective declaration of jurisdictional. The Government is in enough trouble over codfish and the question of jurisdiction in
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
the waters off the east coast of Canada. This question could give us the same kind of jurisdiction squabble all along the border with the United States. Nothing is provided to guard against that.
I want to refer to the matter of safety. I believe Members of the House should take very seriously the experience in the United States as reflected by a recent article written in The New York Times. The dateline is December 6 in Atlanta. It points out that there have been 16 deaths in Atlanta as a result of truck related accidents on the freeways in the metropolitan area, which is up from 12 last year. A one-third increase in truck related deaths is cause for concern and something we should not ignore.
The article by Mr. Schmidt goes on to say:
Partly as a result of deregulation of the trucking industry in 1980, not only are there more trucks but also much larger trucks plying the nation's roads and interstate highways.
Not only more trucks, but bigger trucks will be coming here if we do not pay attention to the experience. He goes on to say:
Safety experts also say that as competition has increased among trucking companies and independents, so has the tendency among truckers to save time and money by ignoring speed laws, cutting corners on vehicle maintenance schedules and circumventing rules on the number of hours drivers may work without resting.
Deregulation has killed people in the United States. Last year four people were killed who would not have been killed but for the growth of carelessness, negligence and bad maintenance that was promoted by deregulation. They are not the only ones who were killed, but an example of what has happened. The article goes on to give the national picture. The number of accidents in the United States involving interstate trucks rose 23.4 per cent in 1985, from 31,628 to 39,030. In other words, there were 4,500 more accidents involving trucks. Do we want this rate of increase here, by copying their deregulation and allowing those unmaintained, unsupervised trucks free entry into Canada?
Regulations for the training of drivers vary from state to state. They are now belatedly trying to introduce in Congress regulations that will control the competence and the standards expected of truck drivers across the United States. However, that is not yet in place, and in the meantime many untrained drivers could be bringing these 18-wheel rigs into Canada, onto our roads. We should not allow anything so uncontrolled and foolish as that. In fact, before these general safety regulations are put in place the federal Government should exercise its constitutional authority and, in fact, constitutional obligation for safety on extra provincial travel.
There are a number of safety concerns that the trucking industry has asked us to execute. Experience tells us that we cannot expect a busy industry to operate safely on the roads without some rules enacted and maintained by the Government. The trucking industry is asking for such things as audit and inspection criteria nationwide, a procedure for audit of

February 5, 1987
Adjournment Debate
employers' records and record systems which include operator profile and driver profile. It recommends hours of service regulations. This was mentioned in the story in The New York Times from Atlanta. There is insufficient control over the hours of service. Of course, tired drivers are not as safe as well rested drivers. The industry recommends commercial vehicle maintenance standards. Improperly maintained vehicles will come from the United States until some standards are enacted. There should be roadside vehicle inspection. Some provinces provide such inspection more than others. We need a nationwide system of roadside vehicle inspection.
There should be a dangerous goods trainer inspection course. Cities like Toronto are being put seriously at risk by the trucking through of dangerous loads such as toxic wastes and explosives. Many types of dangerous loads are being trucked close to if not right through residential areas in Metropolitan Toronto. We need stronger regulations to protect people in those residential areas and others. That was shown last year on the Trans-Canada Highway in western Ontario where there was a spill of quite a poisonous substance because there is not adequate inspection and control over the use of our highways by trucks. That is an obligation of the federal Government and Parliament.
Finally, there is absolutely nothing in the Bill to respond to the urgent demand, not only of the trucking industry but many other industries and Candaians for protection against predatory pricing. These mammoth companies in the United States can raid the trucking industry in Canada, cut prices for a year, run Canadian companies out of business, then charge any price they like because they will have what is, in effect, an oligopoly, with the rule of a few large companies.
There is nothing in this legislation that resembles the antidumping legislation for manufacturing. That is necessary because experience in the United States shows that predatory pricing destroys the smaller companies. They are the sorts of companies that the Government says it wants to encourage. Small businesses and new entrepreneurs will be wiped out by the big companies if there is no legislation to protect against predatory pricing, rate cutting, or dumping as it is called in international manufacturing.
Many Canadians want to raise these matters in the Standing Committee on Transport. What they have to say is more urgent than ever because of the experience in the United States. They also want the Government to be open enough to the truth to allow witnesses to come from the United States and tell us their good and bad experience with deregulation and let Canadians judge what we want to copy and what we want to avoid.
Canadians want to say a great deal more to this Parliament. They want improvements in transportation legislation. They want, particularly, proper safety legislation and proper protection of Canadian companies against predation from across the border. It is not true that Canadians do not want change. However, they want this Bill to go back to the
Committee for hearings throughout the country so that we can get a truly workable transportation Bill.

subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES. (B) REQUEST FOR INCLUSION OF PUNITIVE MEASURES
THE ADMINISTRATION-CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES. (B) REQUEST FOR INCLUSION OF PUNITIVE MEASURES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the adjournment debate today. You will no doubt recall, Madam Speaker, the famous words written for us by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in the Throne Speech of October 1:
My Government shares the expectations of all Canadians that public office holders maintain the highest standards of conduct, especially in the area of conflict of interest. It will be considering proposals which reflect the essential considerations of fairness to the office holder and the protection of the public's interest.
They are very nice words which were said in Parliament some four months ago, but nothing has happened. However, that is not the reason I rise today. On October 10 I asked a question in the House. The reason I asked the question was because I was shocked at what I heard in the Speech from the Throne. Only a year before the Prime Minster, in introducing new conflict of interest guidelines, had said: "These guidelines are the best in the western world". Mind you, that was one of the Prime Minister's more humble days. He could have said they were the best in the galaxy. Be that as it may, if they were the best in the western world, why was it that a year later we needed new guidelines?
I asked that question in the House of Commons.

And I ask the following question: "Mr. Speaker, what is at issue here is the credibility of this Government. It certainly is not a joke. If the Prime Minister is unwilling to answer, will the Deputy Prime Minister give us his assurances that the new rules will include punitive measures so there is no repetition of what we have seen so often is the past coming from this Government"?
I was precisely asking the Government to include in the conflict of interest guideline some punitive measures so that Parliament may be assured of the integrity of the system. And punitive measures are necessary, especially with the Tories in power, Madam Speaker.

On September 9, 1985, the Prime Minister read from a document in the House, which he tabled with a blue ribbon
February 5, 1987_____________________________COMMONS DEBATES________________________________________________3173
around it. I am sure you remember the day, Madam Speaker. He said:
It is a great principle of public administration-I could even say an imperative-that to function effectively the Government and Public Service of a democracy must have the trust and confidence of the public they serve. In order to reinforce that trust, the Government must be able to provide competent management and, above all, to be guided by the highest standards of conduct.
Is that not beautiful, Madam Speaker? He also said:
We have taken great pains to ensure that the new Code leaves no doubt that the ultimate responsibility for the ethical standards of the federal Government rests with the Cabinet and, more particularly, with me.
He said: "with me", Madam Speaker. He said as well, and perhaps that is where the truth is:
Many of these steps are long overdue, and heaven knows, this Government has had cause to regret their absence. But now they are in place, or in the process of being put in place, and we can look forward together to the dawning of a new day of trust and confidence.
I ask Hon. Members opposite, is it the new day we saw during the last two weeks when we heard of all the sordid affairs? Clearly, the question I asked in this House on October 10 deserves a real reply, not the insignificant nonsense of the reply of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski).

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to address the matter of conflict of interest which has been raised by my hon. colleague. He will know that the conflict of interest guidelines which were instituted by this Government were far tougher than any guidelines instituted by the previous Liberal administration. For comparison, the Hon. Member might want to discuss the matter with Madam Caplan, a former Minister of the Ontario Legislature or perhaps Mr. Fontaine, another former Minister of the Ontario Legislature who had to resign under rather unfortunate circumstances.
When the Hon. Member was in the Ontario Legislature, he succeeded in holding back the Liberal Party from Government. When he left, they formed the Government in Ontario. I think that should be put into the hopper too. The new guidelines do not ask with what law firm your brother-in-law is employed. Perhaps they should, in view of the events during the recent week.
I wish to discuss the Hon. Member's question and response. These guidelines require all federal government public office holders to review their personal interests, and their activities, within the standards of public interest required by the Code, and to file statements indicating their compliance. In addition, those in the most senior and sensitive positions may be required to divest themselves of the interests which they hold through a sale at arm's length, or to give them over to the controlling management of a trustee through a blind, frozen, or retention trust arrangement.
It is up to public office holders to review their assets, activities, and interests on an annual basis. At such time as a
Adjournment Debate
new position is accepted, or there is an important change in their personal situation which might have a possible impact on their duties and obligations under the Code, it is up to them to adhere to the strict guidelines in the Code.
I see nothing in conflict with what the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) has said in his answer, nor do I see any conflict when, in the Speech from the Throne, the Government said it was considering new conflict of interest rules. That is something that is in the interest of all Members of Parliament to look at and see how they can be improved. The standards that are asked of us are being widened considerably.
I say without any hesitation, and as a personal statement, that after 10 years of practising as an accountant, and 10 years of practising law, I had no difficulty during any of those 20 years with conflict of interest guidelines, rules, or laws. They were very clear. I say at the same time, and this also is a personal comment, that the net of conflict of interest guidelines which impact on members of the Opposition, members on the government side, and cabinet Ministers is gradually being widened by the media. In this day and age, it is difficult for any Member of Parliament, or any elected representative at the municipal, provincial, or federal level to determine exactly where that conflict of interest line is. It is not black and white any more. I think that is good, and it is healthy because it is in the public interest.
