subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-UNITED STATES MILITARY SUPPORT FOR SALVADORAN GOVERNMENT
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-UNITED STATES MILITARY SUPPORT FOR SALVADORAN GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 29 I raised a question relating to this Government's policy toward El Salvador and to the refugees from that war-torn country. I have received no answer regarding El Salvador.
On Monday of this week the New York Times reported the death of seven civilians in the village of Laguna Seca. They were killed by the Salvadoran air force carrying out that Government's policy of bombing areas where rebels are said to be. They were using, of course, American equipment.
That bombing is part of a recent strategy change by the Duarte Government, and its American advisers. For many years, former Governments relied on death squads and ground-based attacks to attack the rebels, and anyone else who dared to disagree with the Government.

February 5, 1987
Adjournment Debate
The human rights violations were so blatant and prevalent that Canada ceased bilateral aid in 1981. The election of Duarte as seen by our Government is supposed to mark a return to democracy and to bring a serious decrease in human rights violations. Therefore Canada resumed bilateral aid last year over the objections of many non-governmental organizations and Canadian churches which have experience in Guatemala.
A delegation of prominent Canadians visited El Salvador in November and December to investigate the current situation and to evaluate the role that Canada is playing through its aid and its political support. The report of that mission for peace was not encouraging. It indicated;
The present reality in El Salvador stands in sharp contrast to the hopes raised with Duarte's election promises, including the now notorious and bankrupt social pact, with its commitment to dialogue, democratic growth and social economic justice. Instead the Government has refused to proceed with dialogue and negotiations, continued repression, reduced social services, and increased pressure on workers and peasants to pay for the war.
They and many other reliable observers report that human rights violations are again on the rise, with assasinations of civilians, captures, disappearances, and the taking of political prisoners all increasing. They point out that selective and deliberate attacks have taken place on human rights organizations through 1986. They point out that the nature of the conflict has changed.
The civil war is now prosecuted under the United States doctrine of low intensity conflict which, in El Salvador, combines a variety of tactics ranging from physical violence, through psychological violence to individuals, to pervasive social control.
Death squads have been replaced by the bombing of villages in an attempt to dry up the sea in which the guerrillas swim. Thousands and thousands of villagers have been uprooted from their homes by the Salvadoran army and herded into refugee camps near the capital city.
Low intensity warfare uses foreign aid, such as Canada's, as one part of the psychological warfare program. Those who watched the CBC show "Man Alive" last night saw the kind of psychological warfare I am talking about-the army dispensing food in villages to the people who are captive there and not allowed to return to their homes, all to the accompaniment of propaganda and American band music. That is the new kind of human rights violation in El Salvador.
That war and the horrors it brings with it are funded by the Reagan administration which provides El Salvador with the highest per capita aid of any country in the world. That aid pays for both the traditional warfare of planes and bombs and for the new psychological warfare. The U.S. provides military advisers, U.S. piloted reconnaissance flights, and advice on how to market the image of the Duarte Government, but behind that image little has changed.
That is the message brought back by many concerned Canadians visiting that country, but the message that this Government gives is one of approval. That is how this Government helps the United States in its psychological warfare, and that is what the proposal to resume bilateral aid would do.
There is a related issue that concerns us as Canadians. The United States has been deporting Salvadorans who fled their war-torn country at a rate of more than 1,000 per year. Some 3,700 Salvadorans await deportation, with 2,300 being coerced into so-called voluntarily returning and another 1,300 awaiting their sentences.
We Canadians like to think of ourselves as a humanitarian people. We have expressed that time and again through our willingness to aid and to assist those in need. Our programs which are run by non-governmental organizations, churches, and other private groups are second to none in the world. We also like to think of ourselves as a peace-loving people, as people who advance the cause of peace wherever possible. Our Government now has the opportunity to recognize and act on those sentiments to act in accordance with the wishes of the great majority of Canadians who have taken the trouble to inform themselves about what is happening in Central America.
There are three things particularly which Canadians are asking the Government to do. First, and most immediate, it should reaffirm the policy of accepting Salvadorans at the border of the United States when they come to Canada to claim refugee status and of examining them according to our laws to see whether we find they are genuine refugees or whether there is any other humanitarian reason for allowing them to stay in Canada. Rather we should do that than to force them to return to the United States in the hope that the United States might not deport them to El Salvador, a country where many of the deportees from the United States have been murdered, according to American evidence.
Second, the Government should publicly tell its special friends in the American administration that Canadians do not support the American war in Central America, that that war should come to a negotiated end.
Third, the Government should end its aid program to El Salvador, the bilateral program, or better, should direct the aid to the people of El Salvador through Canadian non-governmental organizations with experience in the area under terms and conditions that guarantee that there will be no connection, no control, by the Government of El Salvador, no approval of projects by Duarte and no necessity for people in El Salvador to choose sides in this civil war in order to receive aid.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as concerns military support and intervention by a third party in Central America, the position of Canada is well-known not only to
February 5, 1987

Members of this House, but also to the governments of the United States, the Soviet Union and Cuba, as well as the countries of Central America. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has stated, we deplore the fact that East-West disputes have spread to Central America and we do not approve of any country providing weapons to any faction whatsoever in the region.
In the case of El Salvador, Canada does not favour a military solution to the internal conflict. We promote a dialogue between the Salvadorian Government and the insurgents and regret that the expected third series of discussions between the two parties did not take place last September. However, we hope that these meetings can be held in the near future. On the other hand, we do not believe that legitimacy is equally shared between both parties. The Duarte Government received the support of the population in the 1984

elections which are considered by both Canadian and international observers as reflecting the will of the people.
The issue of the American policy on refugees concerns only the United States. As for our own policy, as explained by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard), it is determined by the particular concerns and needs of Canada. In the past, there have been consultations between the two Governments on this issue and there is no doubt that the process will continue.
